Her section faces the care home’s dining room, where residents could watch the landscape take shape. Their comments and encouragement provided company while she painted, with one man giving her “the side eye and the thumbs up all the time,” she said. “I went in there and talked to everybody. Everybody is so excited,” Jorgensen said. Sarah Sigurdson, co-founder of Cariboo Art Beat, consulted residents about what they wanted to see. Residents suggested horses, wildflowers, mountains, ranching, logging and gold panning, along with details such as a particular red truck. The artists developed those suggestions into a connected design, Jorgensen explained. Some of the horses in Jorgensen’s newest mural carry more than a connection to the Cariboo landscape. They carry memories of animals that mattered to the people who knew them. Jorgensen asked about horses that had been special to care home residents and incorporated them into the mural, offering a way to honour those memories. British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. items.title: [abcnews.com] Bavarian government vows to restore Hitler-era Eagle’s Nest after fire
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Bavaria’s government says it will restore the fire-gutted Eagle’s Nest, the former Nazi retreat in the Bavarian Alps, after officials warned the structure may not be salvageable. The blaze left the Kehlsteinhaus almost completely destroyed. Crews extinguished the last flames on Saturday but had not entered the building because of concerns it could collapse. Police are investigating a 33-year-old German man detained near the scene as firefighters and police drove up the mountain. Prosecutors said a psychiatric assessment found signs of possible mental illness and that investigators were also examining a possible political motive. Police said there was no current indication of other suspects. Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the site would not be left in ruins. Officials have yet to decide what restoration will involve. Herrmann said they would discuss the next steps with local officials, historians and preservationists, and stressed the importance of continuing historical remembrance.

Jennifer Thoss will become mayor of Lytton, British Columbia, after a random draw broke a 45-45 tie with incumbent Denise O’Connor in the Oct. 17 election. A judicial recount at Kamloops Provincial Court on Tuesday confirmed the tally before the draw selected Thoss. Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. A former councillor, she has criticized the pace of recovery and warned that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure could overwhelm Lytton’s reduced tax base. O’Connor defended the need for recovery staff and infrastructure to attract residents. Thoss said after the draw that she would focus on team-building.

Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Supreme Court agrees to review Trudeau government’s Emergencies Act use
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada agreed on Oct. 22 to hear the federal government’s appeal over its 2022 use of the Emergencies Act during protests in Ottawa and at key border crossings. Two lower courts found the invocation unjustified and ruled that it infringed Charter rights. The Supreme Court will also hear cross-appeals on issues raised by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Canadian Constitution Foundation. The government argues that the lower courts judged its decision with hindsight instead of asking whether officials acted reasonably on the information available at the time. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association says Ottawa is trying to relitigate arguments the courts already rejected. A public inquiry reached a different conclusion from the courts, finding in early 2023 that the government met the high legal threshold, though its commissioner said the factual basis was not overwhelming. No hearing date has been set; a hearing is unlikely before spring 2027 and could take place in the fall.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Europe’s record heat drives €17bn economic loss and strains cities
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Europe’s 2026 heatwaves were linked to an estimated €17 billion loss in European Union gross domestic product from April through September, as well as overloaded hospitals, damaged homes and transport disruptions. Separate peer-reviewed research estimated 50,391 heat-related excess deaths across 854 cities, with about 65% attributed to human-caused warming. The study covered urban areas representing roughly 40% of the population in 30 countries. Britain’s hospitals faced demand comparable to a severe winter virus season, while patients overheated in buildings and heat threatened medical equipment. Wildfires damaged homes, transport systems broke down and cooling equipment failed during the summer heat, according to Bloomberg Economics’ assessment.
